title: Chapter 25: The Stamp Lands Wrong
content: Courtroom 2 is too warm, and it is Saturday, and the radiator under the window has been knocking since twenty to nine, and there is a water stain on the ceiling shaped like Ohio.

Wren sits at the petitioner's table with the log on her left and the certified copies squared on her right. Her hands are flat on the table. Flat hands are the only thing she knows how to do with them in a room.

Bram is in the third row on the aisle. Mars is beside him with her lanyard tucked inside her coat, because she is here as a citizen and has filled out the form that says so. Ruthie has shut the diner for the morning and sits behind them with her ledger closed on her knees, which is the loudest thing in the room.
Celia Reeve is at the back, alone, in the grey coat.
At nine the clerk reads the docket into the record. Forty-two numbers. It takes eleven minutes, and the stenographer changes her ribbon halfway.
Judge Neary comes in at four minutes past. He is sixty-odd, with glasses on a chain and the face of a man who has read a great deal of paper and believed very little of it.
"Miss Aubrey."
"Yes."
"You are the petitioner."
"I am."
"You have no counsel."
"No."
"Then tell me what you are asking this court for."
"One word."
"Say it."
"Drowned."
Barrow stands up for the Authority. He is from Columbus and he has a folder with three tabs in it.

"The District does not dispute that a death occurred," Barrow says. "The District disputes that this court has the power to determine its cause. Cause of death is a medical finding. The release was a federal operation. The file remains under review."
"Under review by whom," the judge says.
"By the District."
"The District is the respondent."
"Yes."
"And the review is of the respondent's own conduct."
"Yes."
"Go on."
Wren stands. She has rehearsed this in the boat shed with the door shut and the river going past, and it does not help, because a boat shed is not a room with a stenographer in it.
"Your Honour, I am not asking anybody to decide what the water did. The water did what it did. I am asking the county to write it down."
"That is what a certificate is."
"Then I am asking for a certificate."

Barrow objects, on the same three grounds, and the judge says, "Overruled, Mr. Barrow, and if you say the words under review one more time I will have the clerk read the docket aloud again, and none of us wants that."
"Exhibit B-4," Wren says. "The Authority's own operating review, revised June 2024. Page sixty-one."
The clerk sets it on the easel and turns it around.
"Would you read section five point two aloud, Mr. Barrow."
Barrow reads it. "Pulse releases shall be conducted in daylight, beginning no earlier than thirty minutes after sunrise and ending no later than thirty minutes before sunset."
"Now five point three."
"An audible warning shall be sounded for not less than thirty seconds immediately before each release. The test shall be recorded in the gate log by the operator on duty."
"Now appendix C. The September page. Read the row for the twelfth."
Barrow's jaw works once. "Twenty-one forty-seven. Ninety seconds. Six feet. Siren, dash. Operator, blank."
"Is a dash a word, Mr. Barrow?"
"It is a mark."
"It is a mark in a column that wants a word." The judge turns the page himself. "Who was the operator?"
"The log does not identify one."
"There is a column."
"The column is empty."
"I can see that the column is empty. I am asking why."
And then a bench makes a noise in the third row from the back, and a man stands up.

Theo Marsh is wearing a suit that does not fit him at the shoulders and carrying the blue folder. He has not shaved well. He had come in at midnight and sat at the table until the sky went grey and said he was going to say it. He stands with one hand half raised, like a boy in a classroom who has decided to be wrong out loud.
"Your Honour. I prepared that review."
Ottoline Reeve turns her head. It is the only movement she makes.
"If it please the court," she says, "the District will examine its own engineer."
She stands. She does not need to. A lawyer would stay seated. She stands because she wants the room to see who is asking.
"Mr. Marsh. You prepared the survey for permit B-4417."
"I did."
"You recommended a ninety-second rise."
"I did."
"You scheduled the release of the twelfth of September."
"I did."
"At whose direction?"
"At the district's."
"At mine?"
"At the district's."
Her mouth does not change. She has been doing this since before he could drive.
"The review you signed states that a release outside these conditions would present an unreasonable risk to persons on the water. Did you read that sentence before you signed it?"
"I wrote it."
"And yet you ran a release at night, in September, with no siren test recorded."
"Yes."
"Why?"
Theo looks up at the water stain, which is shaped like Ohio.
"Because at noon the town would have seen it," he says.
The stenographer's keys stop. Then start again.
"Say that again."

"A daylight release requires public notice. A night release requires a siren. The siren had been out since the fourth of July." He opens the folder. His hands are not steady and he does not try to hide it. "I wrote a memorandum on the ninth of July. I sent it to this building. It asked for a horn. A horn is seventy dollars."
"And nobody replaced it."
"Nobody replaced it."
"So you ran the gate without a warning."
"I ran the gate without a warning, and I told them in writing two months before it cost a man his life, and the memorandum is in the file, and the file is in that drawer."
Ottoline does not look at the drawer. She looks at him.
"Mr. Marsh. You understand that this testimony will end your license."
"I understand it."
"Nine years of work."
"Yes."
"And you are giving it to this court because."

"Because there is a dash in a column," Theo says. "A dash is not a lie. I have been signing dashes for nine years, and a dash is what a man writes when he wants to be able to say afterward that he did not write anything."
The room is quiet. Behind Wren, Ruthie's ledger slides off her knees and hits the floor, and Ruthie does not pick it up.
Ottoline stands there a moment longer than she needs to. Then she sits down.
Judge Neary writes for a while.
"Mr. Drane," he says. "Hollis Drane."
Hollis comes up the aisle with his cardigan buttoned wrong and his keys in his hand, and he puts his hand on the book and swears in a voice that does not carry past the first row.
"Mr. Drane, you are the town clerk at the Annex."
"I am."
"How long."
"Nineteen years."
"Do you keep a drawer?"
Hollis's throat moves. "I keep a drawer."
"What is in it?"
"Filings."
"How many?"
"Forty-two, as of this morning."
"Why are they in a drawer?"
"Because they are pending."
"Pending what?"
"Pending a certified cause of death."
"Who certifies a cause of death in this county?"
"The county."
"And who is the county, in that building, at that window?"
Hollis is quiet for a long time. The radiator knocks twice.
"I am the window," he says.
"When a person comes to your window and asks when their father will be written down, what do you tell them?"
"I tell them maybe tomorrow."
The room makes a sound. Not a laugh. It is the sound forty people make when they breathe out at once.
"How long have you been saying that?"
"Nineteen years."
"Do you mean it?"
"No, Your Honour."
"Then why say it?"

"Because I do not know what else to say to a person standing at a window with a paper in their hand." Hollis's eyes are wet and he is not wiping them, which is worse than if he were. "And because a drawer is not a decision. If I stamp them, I have decided. I am not the person who decides."
"You are the person who keeps," the judge says.
"Yes."
"Show the court the drawer."

It takes two deputies and eleven minutes. The drawer comes up from the second desk, bottom left, in a mail crate, and the crate is set on the table in front of the bench, and the judge comes down and reads the tabs aloud, because the record requires it.
"Pike. Voss Rusk. Deeds. Ross. Finch. Nunn."
Wren stands with her hands at her sides and does not sit down.
At the back of the crate there is one folder with nothing in it and a tab in pencil. The judge reads it. He does not read it aloud.
Then he goes up and sits and takes his glasses off and puts them on the desk.
"The court will take twenty minutes."
At twenty past eleven he comes back and reads for nine minutes without stopping.

He finds that the release was operated at 9:47 p.m. on 12 September 2026, outside the conditions of permit B-4417. He finds that the audible warning was not tested and did not sound. He finds that Elias Aubrey entered the water from the ferry in the course of securing the vessel, and that the release was a contributing cause of his death.
Then he takes his glasses off again.

"The court is asked to certify the cause as drowned. The court cannot. There is no medical certificate in this file. The attending note reads cardiac arrest following immersion. No autopsy was performed, because this death was not classified as reportable by the office that classifies deaths."
"The word the statute provides for a death caused by the lawful act of another, without intent, is misadventure. It is a poor word for a man on his own ferry. It is the word the court has."

"The certificate will issue today. It will be entered with these findings attached, and the findings will name the gate, the permit, and the hour. The clerk will transmit a copy of this order and exhibit B-4 to the Division of Water Resources for review of permit B-4417, and will do so before he goes home."
"The remaining forty-one matters are held open without prejudice. The court notes that it has no medical evidence in any of them either, and that the absence is not an accident of nature."
The clerk stamps four times. The sound is the small wet sound Wren has heard all autumn, and it lands on her grandfather's name.
"Your Honour."
"Miss Aubrey."
"May I say one thing for the record."
"Say it."

"The box says misadventure." She has the certificate in her hand and she does not look at it. "My grandfather did not misadventure. He was on his own boat, in his own river, doing the thing he did for fifty-one years. A gate that was not allowed to run at night ran at night. That is not a misadventure. That is a word somebody picked because it fit the box."
The judge looks at her. He is not unkind. That is the worst part.
"The finding says all of that," he says. "The finding is certified and attached."
"The finding is a paragraph. The box is the word."
"Yes," he says. "That is how a record works."
Outside the steps are wet with salt and the whole east side of Market Street is standing on them.
The reporter from the county paper gets to her before she has her gloves on.
"Miss Aubrey. Are you relieved?"
"No."
"What did you get?"
"A sentence."
He writes it down. "Forty-one still pending."
"Forty-one."

She goes down the steps with the certified copy folded in her coat and stops at the bottom, and reads the box in the flat grey light. MISADVENTURE. Twelve letters. There is room in the box for twenty.
Behind her, Barrow is already on his phone with his hand cupped against the wind, and he says the word settlement twice, and she hears both times.
highlight: Theo testifies, Hollis admits the drawer, and the certificate comes back stamped misadventure.
